title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Introduction
content: Transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS) is a cornerstone in the evaluation of the prostate. The technique was first described in 1963 by Takahashi et al and was later used for prostate cancer detection by Gotoh and Nishi in 1965. [1] [2] [3] However, the technique was not widely used until 1985, when 5 MHz transrectal probes became available. [4] TRUS is now commonly used for imaging prostatic pathology, especially benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostate cancer, possible prostatic abscesses, and prostatitis, as well as providing visual guidance for prostate biopsies. [5]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Introduction
content: BPH is extremely prevalent, with 80% of men being affected by age 70. [6] Imaging is not required for diagnosis, which is typically based on clinical signs, symptom score, post-void residual urine volume, digital rectal examination (DRE) results, pressure/flow studies, and/or cystoscopy. [6] However, changes in the prostate are easily recognized on TRUS, and it may be recommended for anatomical evaluation and volume measurements to help with surgical decision-making and determination of PSA density for cancer screening if any surgical intervention is planned. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Introduction
content: Prostate cancer is the most common new cancer diagnosis in men, and the incidence is only expected to increase as the population ages. [12] The widespread worldwide routine monitoring of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has greatly increased the overall diagnosis rate of prostate cancer. [12] However, these are mostly low-grade neoplasms frequently treated with active surveillance. [12] TRUS is the most widely used imaging tool to evaluate prostate cancer, as it serves as the primary guide for prostate biopsies. [12] About 1 million prostate biopsies are performed in the United States and 3 million worldwide every year, making it one of the most commonly performed urological procedures for men. [2] [13]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The prostate is a male genitourinary organ located between the bladder and the urogenital diaphragm. This organ is shaped like a walnut and measures on average 3.75 to 4.0 × 2.5 to 3.0 × 3.1 to 3.8 cm (width × length × height) with a normal volume of 20 to 30 cc. [17] The prostatic base is adjacent to the bladder neck, with its apex at the urogenital diaphragm. [17] The prostate extends from the bladder neck proximally to the membranous urethra (external sphincter) distally and wholly surrounds the prostatic urethra. [17] [18]

[17] The puboprostatic ligament supports the prostate anteriorly, and the membranous urethra provides distal stability. [17] Proximally, the prostate is contiguous with the bladder at the bladder neck, where the internal urinary sphincter is located. [18] The prostate sits above the urogenital diaphragm and is surrounded by the puborectal portion of the levator ani muscle. [17]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The seminal vesicles are paired hypoechoic sacs that join with the ampulla of the vas deferens at the posterior aspect of the prostate to form the paired ejaculatory ducts, which traverse the gland posteriorly and empty into the prostatic urethra at the verumontanum. [17] [19] [20] [21] [22] Each seminal vesicle measures  about 2 cm in length. [17] [19] Although they act as direct extensions, the ejaculatory ducts lack the thick muscular walls of the seminal vesicles. [20] These ejaculatory ducts are typically <2.4 mm in diameter unless pathologically dilated. [20]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The prostate is most commonly classified into anatomic zones—the peripheral, central, transitional, and periurethral zones, in addition to the anterior fibromuscular stroma, which contains non-glandular tissue. [17] The peripheral zone accounts for 70% of the prostate's mass and is where most prostate cancers arise. [6] Prostate cancer is unique in that it is typically multifocal, whereas most other malignancies tend to be unifocal unless they have metastasized. [12] The central zone contains glandular tissue, where the ejaculatory ducts travel to empty into the posterior prostatic urethra. [17] This zone is the most common for prostatitis. [23] The transitional zone is the smallest component and surrounds the urethra. This zone is the primary site of BPH. [17]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Functionally, the prostate has a set of paired lateral lobes and a median lobe. Enlargement of these prostatic lobes by BPH leads to voiding difficulties, obstructive uropathy, and a variety of lower urinary tract symptoms. [17] The median lobe can grow intravesically, where it can be detected by transabdominal ultrasonography. Depending on the size and shape of this median lobe extension, it may also act as a ball valve, interfering with normal micturition. [6]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The prostate is supplied by 3 branches of the internal iliac arteries—the internal pudendal, inferior vesicle, and middle rectal arteries. [17] The prostate receives venous blood from the dorsal vein of the penis and drains into the iliac veins. There is also a communication to the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), which accounts for the metastatic spread of prostate cancer to the vertebral bodies. [17] The lymphatic drainage is primarily to the internal iliac and sacral lymph nodes. [17] This drainage receives parasympathetic supply from pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-4) and sympathetic supply from the inferior hypogastric plexuses. [17] The neurovascular bundle travels posterolateral to the prostate. [17]

content: The primary function of the prostate is reproductive, as it produces a secretion that constitutes about 25% of the semen. The glandular prostatic tissue produces the glycoprotein PSA, which liquefies semen, citrate, multiple prostaglandins (A, E, and F), prostatic acid phosphatase, spermidine, spermine, and zinc. [24] [25] All of these are important in protecting and mobilizing sperm. [24]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Indications
content: TRUS-guided prostate biopsies are frequently used for patients suspected of having prostate cancer due to hard nodules on DRE or persistently elevated PSA levels. [27] [28] Any patient with unexplained, persistently elevated PSA levels; a hard, suspicious nodule on DRE; or hypoechoic areas on transrectal prostatic ultrasound, especially in the peripheral zone, should undergo a prostatic biopsy. [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Prostate Cancer Screening ," for further information.

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Indications
content: Although there are many indications, TRUS is most often used for guidance in prostatic biopsies, aquablation therapy for BPH, prostatic brachytherapy, and placement of fiduciary markers before radiation therapy for prostate cancer. Indications for TRUS of the prostate include the following: Aquabation or similar ultrasound-guided therapy for BPH Estimation of prostate size when treatment is needed for BPH Evaluation and aspiration of suspected prostatic abscesses Evaluation for an unexplained, persistently elevated PSA or a hard prostatic nodule suspicious for prostatic cancer on DRE Evaluation of selected cases of persistent hematospermia High-intensity focused ultrasound treatment of prostate cancer or BPH Male infertility Placement of fiduciary markers before external beam radiation therapy for prostate cancer Prostatic brachytherapy for cancer Prostatic cryotherapy Transrectal or transperineal prostate biopsy [33]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Contraindications
content: There are no prostatic conditions that constitute absolute contraindications to TRUS. However, probe insertion may be precluded by unrelated anorectal pathologies, including rectal masses, malignancies, hemorrhoids, anal fissures, dermatologic lesions, prior rectal surgery, or strictures. These factors are typically evaluated during the pre-procedural DRE. [22]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Equipment
content: This technique uses endorectal linear or convex transducers with high frequencies (7.5-10 MHz is acceptable; however, higher-frequency transducers are preferred for better resolution). [34] [35] Both single-plane and biplane transducers may be used; however, biplane transducers are preferred, as they do not require exchanging probes to view both axial and sagittal planes necessary for a complete evaluation, thereby decreasing the patient's overall discomfort. [34] The ability to simultaneously view both sagittal imaging with the projected biopsy need track and axial imaging for spatial orientation is a significant advantage of using biplanar transducers. content: Color and power Doppler are widely available tools for assessing vascularity. [36] These tools are particularly useful for evaluating inflammatory conditions, blood flow, or overall tissue vascularity. [36] [37] Elastography is an emerging technology that helps identify differences in tissue stiffness, such as in the relatively stiff prostate tissue associated with prostate cancer. [38] Three-dimensional ultrasonography provides a more detailed view of the prostate, allowing evaluation in the coronal plane and clarifying the spatial relationships of the prostatic capsule and adjacent structures. [39] [40] Contrast-enhanced ultrasound uses microbubble ultrasonographic contrast agents to better demonstrate tissue enhancement and neovascularity with increased vascular density generally associated with malignancy. [41] [42] [43] [44]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Equipment
content: If the ultrasound is being performed to guide a prostate biopsy, the preferred probe is a biplanar transducer with axial and sagittal imaging capabilities. Being able to simultaneously view the axial plane (for right and left orientation) and the sagittal without changing transducers is highly advantageous. The probe must contain an internal bioptic channel or attached biopsy needle guide, corresponding to the needle track demonstrated on the ultrasound screen in sagittal mode. [33] [45]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Personnel
content: When performing TRUS-guided biopsies, a trained assistant is essential. The assistant's responsibilities include removing each specimen after collection, placing it in the appropriately labeled container, sterilizing the needle tip by briefly dipping it in formalin (optional but recommended), re-cocking the biopsy gun, resetting the safety, and carefully handing the device back to the urologist.

[46] Nevertheless, a simple mechanical cleansing of the rectum immediately before TRUS seems reasonable to reduce artifacts, improve imaging, evacuate feces, eliminate gas, and reduce the risk of infection with minimal risk or significant patient discomfort. title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Transrectal Ultrasonography
content: Contrast enhancement uses injected microbubble contrast agents that harmlessly pass through the pulmonary vasculature due to their small size (<1 µm), thereby enhancing the visualization of end organs, such as the prostate. [98] [99] [105] [106] [107] [108] [109] [110] [111] [112] Enhancement after bolus injection typically lasts only 1 to 2 minutes; slow intravenous infusion can extend this enhancement. Imaging is usually performed with Doppler or grayscale harmonic settings. However, newer techniques (intermittent harmonic imaging or flash-replenishment technique) may also allow for increased contrast penetration into the prostate. Intermittent harmonic imaging uses a slower frame rate, thereby prolonging microbubble survival and allowing for better visualization of the microvascularity associated with prostate cancer. [45] [110] [112] [113] [114] Flash replenishment uses high-power ultrasonography to destroy the microbubbles, followed by low-power pulses to visualize vascular replenishment. This imaging technique provides detailed visualization of the prostatic vasculature, enabling the accurate targeting of biopsies. [45] [115] [116]

content: PSA density: The PSA density is determined by dividing the PSA value by the prostatic volume. [127] A higher PSA density suggests prostatic malignancy; lower values indicate BPH. [127] An abnormal PSA density, as defined by international consensus, is generally considered to be any value greater than 0.15 ng/mL/cc. However, higher cutoff values, such as≥0.18 ng/mL/cc, ≥0.20 ng/mL/cc, and even 0.30 ng/mL/cc, have been suggested by various studies. [128] [129] [130] [131] [132] [133] The PSA density is a useful parameter, but it is not definitive. The PSA density is best used in conjunction with physical examination findings, clinical symptoms, imaging results, bioassay risk stratification tests, and other relevant data to determine the likelihood of malignancy and whether a prostatic biopsy should be performed. content: Color or power Doppler may show increased blood flow; however, this is not a highly sensitive method and is typically observed only in higher-grade cancers. [36] [98] [99] Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography can reveal increased blood flow due to the tumor's higher microvessel density. Because of increased cell density and stiffness, prostate cancer exhibits decreased elasticity, aiding in diagnosis and guiding biopsies. [98] [107] [108] Grayscale imaging can evaluate tumor extent and may show bulges, irregularities of the prostatic contour, and disrupted periprostatic fat. A hyperechoic seminal vesicle, asymmetric enlargement, or anterior displacement (altered prostate-seminal vesicle angle) suggests seminal vesicle involvement. Prostatic MRI provides superior differentiation of suspicious prostatic nodules from benign tissue and is preferred over ultrasound for diagnostic cancer imaging, evaluation of extracapsular extension, and assessment of regional lymph node involvement.

content: Prostatic cysts: These cysts are often detected on prostatic ultrasonography. These cysts become clinically significant if they interfere with male fertility. Congenital cysts may originate from either Müllerian or Wolffian ducts. Persistent Müllerian duct cysts appear as midline, anechoic cystic structures with a teardrop shape when viewed in the sagittal plane. These cysts are often associated with hypospadias (11% of hypospadias patients), but can be as high as 40% in patients with posterior hypospadias. [79] The incidence of Müllerian duct cysts increases with higher grades of hypospadias, as the urethral meatus becomes more proximal or posterior. [138] [139] [140] [141] [142]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Biopsy Technique
content: Standard prostate biopsies typically include about 12 samples. [201] [202] This number is a reasonable compromise between obtaining adequate prostate sampling, post-biopsy complication rate, infection risk, and patient discomfort. [47] [201] [202] [203] A common approach is to obtain two samples each from the base, mid-gland, and apex of both lobes, yielding 12 biopsy cores placed in 6 specimen jars. [204] Repeated sampling of the same site should be avoided; for subsequent passes, the needle should be redirected slightly to a different location. Taking additional biopsy samples in patients with larger prostates appears reasonable. [205] Extra lateral core samples increase the cancer detection rate. [206] Increasing the number of samples from 12 to 18 in prostates weighing more than 55 g has been suggested. [205] Additional samples from the transition zone do not increase the cancer detection rate. [47] [207] Routine biopsies of the seminal vesicles are not indicated. [47] [207]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Biopsy Technique
content: After the biopsy procedure, the probe is slowly and gently withdrawn, and a small gauze pad, pack, or dressing is applied to the rectum. The patient is told to sit up carefully and observed for a short period, usually less than 30 minutes, with several vital signs readings periodically to monitor for abnormal changes and excessive rectal bleeding. The patient is told to expect some rectal and urinary bleeding. The patient is instructed to notify the clinician if the bleeding becomes excessive, a fever develops, or any other problems arise. If PiRAD 3, 4, or 5 lesions have been detected on MRI, the ultrasound biopsy technique can be combined with MRI using digital overlay, allowing for visualization in an MRI fusion biopsy. [216] [217] Biopsies of the MRI-targeted lesions should be performed first and labeled separately, followed by the standard sextant sampling. [218] The patient is typically given a return appointment to review the biopsy results about 1 week later.

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Transrectal Versus Transperineal Prostate Biopsies
content: The European Association of Urology has already recommended transperineal prostatic biopsies over transrectal biopsies in their 2021 Guidelines. [91] [219] Both techniques use TRUS for imaging; however, the perineal approach typically uses a fixed external template to guide transperineal biopsies, although it can also be performed freehand. By avoiding transrectal biopsies and inoculating fecal material into the highly vascular prostate, post-procedure infectious complications are reduced from 5% to 7% (urinary tract infections) and 1% to 3% (sepsis) to 0. [13] [91] [220] Complications such as rectal bleeding, fever, and urinary retention are substantially reduced with transperineal biopsies. [221] [222]

content: MRI uses a strong magnetic field to cause water molecules within organs and other bodily structures to align or line up. [250] This alignment is temporarily disrupted when the tissue is exposed to pulsed radio waves of the right frequency. [250] In between the pulsed radio waves, when the signals are briefly turned off, the water molecules lose their alignment but quickly realign when the radio wave returns, emitting a distinctive radio signal. This tissue-generated signal is picked up by antennas in the MRI machine and used by a computer to generate an MRI image. [250]

content: Diffusion-weighted imaging: This reading represents the random movement of water molecules within the various zones of the prostate. Malignant tissue has increased cellularity, restricting free water movement compared to normal tissue or BPH. [254] [255] Lesions are scored based on the diffusion-weighted imaging signal intensity compared to normal tissue within the same zone. [254] [255] Normal prostate or BPH appears dark on diffusion-weighted imaging and bright on ADC mapping, indicating relatively unrestricted free water diffusion. Prostate cancer typically exhibits a bright signal on diffusion-weighted imaging, accompanied by a dark image on ADC mapping, indicating focal areas of densely packed cells where water diffusion is restricted, which are more likely to be malignant.

content: Dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging : Immediately after the injection of contrast media (typically gadolinium, which changes the magnetic properties of nearby water molecules, making them clearer and brighter on MRI), multiple serial MRI images are collected. Prostate cancers, with their enhanced vascularity, typically show faster and earlier tissue enhancement and quicker washout compared to normal tissue. title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- PI-RADS scoring:
content: PI-RADS 1: Cancer risk is minimal and highly unlikely. Normal T2WI, diffusion-weighted imaging, and ADC mapping appear normal. There may be round, fully encapsulated nodules (BPH) in the transitional zone, but only uniform, homogeneous images are present in the peripheral zone. [12] [18] [260] A biopsy is not recommended solely based on the PI-RADS score. [260] [261] PI-RADS 2: Cancer risk is low and considered unlikely. Findings may include heterogeneity on T2WI and hypointensity of the peripheral zone on diffusion-weighted imaging. A mostly encapsulated or circumscribed nodule may exist without encapsulation (atypical nodule) in the transitional zone. Mild hypointense homogeneous imaging may be present between nodules. The peripheral zone may have linear or wedge-shaped hypointense or diffusely mild hypointense signal nodules, typically with indistinct margins. [12] [18] [260] A biopsy is not recommended solely based on the PI-RADS score. [260] [261]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment
content: PI-RADS 3: Cancer risk is moderate and considered equivocal. Findings may include heterogeneous lesions with indistinct margins on T2WI. Nodules appear hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging and hypointense on ADC, with focal areas of mild-to-moderate hypointensity on ADC or mild hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging. A lesion may exhibit either significant hypointensity on ADC or significant hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging, but not both. The lesion does not meet the criteria for any other PI-RADS category. [12] [18] [260] A biopsy is recommended based on the PI-RADS score. [260] [261] For peripheral zone lesions otherwise classified as PI-RADS 3, positive findings on dynamic contrast enhancement upgrade the classification to PI-RADS 4. [12] [18] [260] Positive findings on dynamic contrast enhancement include early or simultaneous enhancement of adjacent normal prostatic tissues corresponding to the suspicious finding on T2WI or diffusion-weighted imaging. [12] [18] [260] [262] Early contrast washout is also a positive finding. [12] [18] [260] Considering the PSA density value can help avoid unnecessary biopsies safely in this equivocal PI-RADS classification. [133] [263] [264] [265] [266] [267]

content: PI-RADS 4: Cancer risk is high and considered likely. A nodule may be a lenticular or non-circumscribed lesion less than 1.5 cm in maximum size in the transitional zone or a circumscribed nodule less than 1.5 cm in the peripheral zone. Lesions are moderately homogeneous and hypointense on T2WI, hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging, and hypointense on ADC. [260] [261]

content: As a general rule, PI-RADS 3, 4, and 5 lesions are biopsied using MRI fusion-guided techniques, whereas a standard TRUS-guided procedure is used for PI-RADS 1 and 2 lesions. [12] [27] [269] Some recent studies suggest that PI-RADS 3 lesions may not require targeted MRI fusion-guided biopsies, as the incidence of clinically significant prostate cancer detected in these specified areas is quite small, and a standard TRUS-guided procedure is sufficient. [270] [271] Biopsies may be omitted in patients with PI-RADS 3 lesions who have a PSA density (PSA/prostate volume cc) below 0.15, which could prevent up to 48% of unnecessary procedures. [272] [273]

content: Prostate malignancies are most often found in the peripheral zone. Typical imaging features include T2WI hypointensity (hypoechoic), low ADC values (dark, hypointense), high diffusion-weighted imaging readings (bright, hyperintense), and positive findings on dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging. The PI-RADS imaging score categorizes these findings into a single, easily understood score. Patients with PI-RADS 3, 4, or 5 lesions should generally have an MRI fusion-guided prostate biopsy. [12] [18] [260]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Magnetic Resonance Imaging Fusion-Guided Prostate Biopsies
content: When MRI imaging shows suspicious (PI-RADS 3, 4, or 5) lesions, the radiologist electronically outlines and digitally colors them. Although biopsies can be performed directly in the MRI machine itself, most often an MRI fusion-guided TRUS biopsy is performed. With its suspicious areas marked, outlined, and colored by the radiologist, the MRI image is digitally superimposed, fused, and correlated with the live prostatic TRUS. [216] [217] [218] [274] [275]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Technique or Treatment -- Magnetic Resonance Imaging Fusion-Guided Prostate Biopsies
content: This MRI fusion-guided technique enables the biopsy to be performed in the same manner as the standard biopsy procedure described above, with the added benefit that suspicious lesions identified on the MRI are now visible and highlighted on the TRUS image for targeted core sampling. [216] [217] [218] The digital MRI image, with its colored target lesions, can be electronically superimposed, overlaid, and correlated with the real-time transrectal prostatic ultrasound picture, making the suspicious areas from the MRI visible during TRUS. With the MRI correlated and superimposed on the live ultrasound image, directed biopsies of the suspicious lesions can now be performed using TRUS. At least 2, but typically 3 or 4, samples are taken from every suspicious lesion identified by MRI. Typically, a standard 12-core sextant biopsy sampling is performed in addition to biopsies of the suspicious lesions identified on the MRI. [218]

content: Shear wave elastography: This technique has similar sensitivity and specificity for prostate cancer detection as MRI. [284] [285] [286] Prostate cancers tend to be harder and denser than normal tissue. Elastography can measure the increased firmness and stiffness of malignant prostatic tissue with good diagnostic results, similar to prostatic MRI. [284] [285] [286] Although multiparametric prostatic MRI has become the standard of care for screening patients with elevated PSA levels and possible prostate cancer, elastography may still play a useful role in equivocal or borderline cases. [287]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Complications
content: There are no known complications from transrectal prostate ultrasonography. However, there are potential complications if the ultrasound is performed in conjunction with a transrectal prostate biopsy, such as hematospermia (93%), hematuria (65%), rectal bleeding (37%), erectile dysfunction (34%), urinary tract infection (15%), urinary retention (6%), and sepsis (1%). [46] [290] [291] [292] [293] [294] Although these are encountered relatively frequently, they are typically mild and self-limited, except for sepsis, which is uncommon. [291] [292] [293] [295] Other complications include epididymitis, orchitis, pain, and prostatitis. [46] [290] [291] The incidence of these complications tends to rise as the number of biopsy samples increases. [292] [296]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Complications
content: Differentiating prostate cancer from BPH solely based on ultrasonographic findings can be quite challenging, especially if the malignant pathology is located anteriorly, in the central zone, or in the transitional zone. [292] [297] In such cases, multiparametric prostatic MRI is suggested to optimize targeting. If no suspicious lesions are detected on MRI, proceed with standard TRUS-guided sextant biopsies if there is sufficient suspicion based on clinical parameters, history, or laboratory results. [12] [27] [134]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Complications
content: Pain management is a significant issue in performing transrectal biopsies. Careful probe insertion, use of pre-biopsy rectal analgesics, adequate lubrication, gentle handling to avoid excessive manipulation, effective periprostatic and apical anesthetic blocks, and allowing sufficient time for anesthesia to take effect are key measures for minimizing patient pain and discomfort. [292] This pain can last for several hours after the procedure. [292] Risk factors for increased pain include the number of biopsy samples taken, prostatic volume, and younger age. [292] [294] Combination anesthesia protocols have demonstrated superior pain relief compared to single modality analgesia and are therefore recommended. [170] [292] [300] [301] Periprostatic nerve blocks may rarely cause vasovagal syncope. [156] [170] [172] [292] [302] [303] [304] [305]

[292] Alternatively, patients may be converted to a transperineal biopsy approach, although TRUS is still required. [292]

title: Transrectal Ultrasonography and Image-Guided Biopsies of the Prostate -- Clinical Significance
content: TRUS of the prostate is an essential tool in the evaluation of prostatic pathology. Understanding the techniques enables the ordering of appropriate tests for the correct scenarios, potentially in situations that may not have been recommended in the past. Advancing techniques also enable better diagnosis and reduce the need for cross-sectional CT imaging, which involves exposure to ionizing radiation.
